pos: v. (to esteem as worthless; to look down upon; rendering Hebrew bazah, Greek kataphroneo, exoutheneo)
etymology: From Latin despicio, to look down upon. The word is a verdict of the eye: to despise a thing is to appraise it and price it at nothing, which is why Scripture uses it of how men valued the Messiah.
biblical_def: To despise is to reckon a thing worthless, and Scripture's gravest use of the word describes the world's valuation of Christ: “He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not” (Isaiah 53:3). The prophet does not say He was hated, which would at least concede importance; He was not esteemed, priced at nothing, passed over. The same verb measures what God will not do with a broken man: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Psalm 51:17). What men throw away, God receives. Turned toward instruction, despising marks the fool by definition: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction” (Proverbs 1:7). Folly here is not ignorance but appraisal — the fool has weighed wisdom and found it not worth having. Paul applies the word to the most dangerous form of contempt, which wears the face of comfort: “Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?” (Romans 2:4). Patience unrepented of is patience despised.
webster_summary: To contemn; to scorn; to disdain; to have the lowest opinion of. Scripture uses it of men despising the Messiah, of God refusing to despise a contrite heart, of fools despising wisdom, and of sinners despising the goodness that leads to repentance.
webster_full: DESPISE, v.t. [L. despicio; de and specio, to look.] To contemn; to scorn; to disdain; to have the lowest opinion of.
2. To abhor; to slight; to neglect as unworthy of regard.
3. To undervalue; to esteem lightly; as, to despise riches or honors.
DESPISED, pp. Contemned; scorned; disdained; neglected.
DESPISER, n. A contemner; a scorner; one who slights or undervalues.
DESPICABLE, a. That may be or deserves to be despised; contemptible; mean; vile; worthless.
scriptures: Isaiah 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
Psalm 51:17
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
Proverbs 1:7
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Romans 2:4
Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?
corruption_summary: Contempt has been redistributed: it is thought shameful to despise anything the age approves, and unremarkable to despise the wisdom, the reproof, and the forbearance that Scripture says only a fool prices at nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: The age is sensitive to contempt directed at persons and blind to contempt directed at truth. To despise a man is rightly held to be wrong; to despise instruction, correction, and the accumulated wisdom of the fathers is treated as independence of mind. Proverbs 1:7 divides the two plainly. The fool is not defined by low intelligence but by his appraisal — he has looked at wisdom and priced it at nothing. That contempt is invisible to the man holding it, because it feels like discernment; and it is unteachable, because instruction is the very thing being despised.

The subtlest despising is the one Romans 2:4 names, and almost nobody recognizes it as contempt at all. God's goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering delay a judgment that is deserved; and the man who takes the delay as evidence that nothing is owed has not merely misread the delay but insulted it. Presumption is contempt wearing the face of comfort. Isaiah 53:3 shows where such appraisal finally lands: it was not rage that met the Messiah but the settled verdict that He was not worth esteeming. Recover the true scale, and a man will fear despising the patience of God more than he fears the scorn of men.
roots_summary: Hebrew bazah (to despise, to hold in contempt) governs Isaiah 53:3 and Psalm 51:17; Greek kataphroneo (to think down upon) and exoutheneo (to count as nothing) carry the New Testament sense.
roots_lines: Hebrew bazah (H959) — to despise, disdain, hold in contempt; the verb of the despised Servant in Isaiah 53:3.
Hebrew ma'ac (H3988) — to reject, refuse, spurn; the companion word for casting a thing away as worthless.
Greek kataphroneo (G2706) — to think down upon, to despise; the verb of Romans 2:4 for despising God's goodness.
Greek exoutheneo (G1848) — to make of no account, to set at nought; used of despising a brother and of the base things God chose.
Hebrew muwcar (H4148) — instruction, correction, discipline; the thing fools despise in Proverbs 1:7.
usage: “He was despised, and we esteemed him not” — the verdict was not hatred but a price of nothing.
“A broken and a contrite heart… thou wilt not despise” — what men discard God receives.
“Despisest thou the riches of his goodness” — presumption is contempt for divine patience.

pos: n. (violent anger; rage; rendering Hebrew chemah, Greek thumos)
etymology: From Latin furor, rage or madness. Scripture is careful with the word: God's fury is settled judicial heat against sin, never the loss of self-possession, and the fury of men is exactly that loss.
biblical_def: Fury renders a Hebrew word for burning heat, and Scripture applies it to God and to men in ways that must be kept distinct. In God it is judicial, announced beforehand, and avoidable by repentance: “Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart… lest my fury come forth like fire, and burn that none can quench it, because of the evil of your doings” (Jeremiah 4:4). The fury is conditional upon impenitence and is preceded by a call to circumcise the heart. It is also purposeful rather than uncontrolled: “I will cause my fury to rest upon them… and they shall know that I the LORD have spoken it in my zeal” (Ezekiel 5:13). And it can be truly denied of Him toward His own vineyard: “Fury is not in me: who would set the briers and thorns against me in battle?” (Isaiah 27:4). In men the same word describes the collapse of self-command, and Scripture gives it a face: “Then was Nebuchadnezzar full of fury, and the form of his visage was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego: therefore he spake, and commanded that they should heat the furnace one seven times more than it was wont to be heated” (Daniel 3:19). Fury altered his countenance and made him foolish, since a furnace seven times hotter did not touch the three men at all.
webster_summary: Rage; violent anger; madness; turbulence. Scripture distinguishes the LORD's fury — judicial, declared beforehand, and turned aside by repentance — from the fury of men, which disfigures the face and unseats the reason.
webster_full: FURY, n. [L. furia, from furo, to rage.] A storm of anger; madness; rage; a violent passion of the mind.
2. Enthusiasm; heat of the mind; as, poetic fury.
3. Violence; impetuous motion; as, the fury of the winds or of a tempest.
4. In mythology, a deity represented as an avenging spirit; hence, a turbulent, violent woman.
FURIOUS, a. Rushing with impetuosity; violent; raging; mad; transported with passion.
FURIOUSLY, adv. With impetuous motion or agitation; violently; vehemently.
scriptures: Jeremiah 4:4

Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart, ye men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: lest my fury come forth like fire, and burn that none can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.
Ezekiel 5:13

Thus shall mine anger be accomplished, and I will cause my fury to rest upon them, and I will be comforted: and they shall know that I the LORD have spoken it in my zeal, when I have accomplished my fury in them.
Isaiah 27:4
Fury is not in me: who would set the briers and thorns against me in battle? I would go through them, I would burn them together.
Daniel 3:19

Then was Nebuchadnezzar full of fury, and the form of his visage was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego: therefore he spake, and commanded that they should heat the furnace one seven times more than it was wont to be heated.
corruption_summary: God's fury is now widely treated as an embarrassment to be explained away as ancient projection, while men's fury is excused as authenticity — an exact reversal of Scripture's judgment on both.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is to apologize for the wrath of God, treating passages like Ezekiel 5:13 as a primitive people's projection of their own violence onto heaven. The texts resist that handling. God's fury in Scripture is never impulsive, never disproportionate, and never uninformed; it is announced in advance, its cause is named, its remedy is offered, and it accomplishes a stated purpose so that men “shall know that I the LORD have spoken it”. Remove it and nothing better is left in its place: a God with no settled heat against evil is a God indifferent to the wronged, and the cross becomes an extravagance answering no real necessity.

At the same time the age has grown tender toward human fury, which it renames passion or authenticity and treats as evidence of sincerity. Daniel 3:19 gives the biblical portrait instead: Nebuchadnezzar's fury changed the form of his visage and drove him to heat a furnace sevenfold, which accomplished precisely nothing except the deaths of his own men. Scripture's counsel is consistent — the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God, and he that is slow to anger is better than the mighty. Recover both halves: fear the fury of God, which is just; distrust your own, which disfigures.
roots_summary: Hebrew chemah (heat, rage, fury) is the burning-heat word used of both God and men; 'aph (nostril, anger) and Greek thumos (passionate heat) fill out the field.
roots_lines: Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, burning anger, fury; the word in Jeremiah 4:4 and Ezekiel 5:13.
Hebrew 'aph (H639) — nostril, face, anger; the physical image behind the biblical language of wrath.
Hebrew qin'ah (H7068) — zeal, jealousy; the disposition Ezekiel names as the ground of the LORD's speaking.
Aramaic chema (H2528) — fury, rage; the word describing Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 3:19.
Greek thumos (G2372) — passion, heat of anger; distinguished from orge, settled wrath, in the New Testament.
usage: “Lest my fury come forth like fire” — divine fury is announced beforehand and may be turned aside.
“Fury is not in me” — the LORD can truly deny fury toward His own vineyard.
“Full of fury, and the form of his visage was changed” — human fury disfigures and unseats reason.

pos: adj. (violent; savage; vehement; rendering Hebrew 'az, charown, Greek anemeros)
etymology: From Latin ferus, wild or savage. Scripture uses the word of beasts, of winds, of nations sent in judgment, and of the last days' men — and once, solemnly, of the anger of the day of the LORD.
biblical_def: Fierce names a violence that is untamed rather than merely strong. Jacob pronounces it upon his own sons' rage and curses the thing without cursing the men: “Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7). The dying patriarch distinguishes anger from its fierceness, and it is the fierceness he condemns. In the covenant curses fierceness becomes a national instrument, described by its face and by what it will not do: “A nation of fierce countenance, which shall not regard the person of the old, nor shew favour to the young” (Deuteronomy 28:50). Mercilessness toward the aged and the child is the mark of the thing. The prophets apply the same adjective to the day of judgment itself: “Behold, the day of the LORD cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate: and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it” (Isaiah 13:9). And the Apostle sets it in his catalogue of the last days, between two other symptoms of a society coming apart: men shall be “without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good” (2 Timothy 3:3).
webster_summary: Vehement; violent; furious; savage; ravenous. Scripture applies the word to cursed anger, to nations of merciless countenance, to the day of the LORD's judgment, and to the character of men in the last days.
webster_full: FIERCE, a. [L. ferus, wild, savage.] Vehement; violent; furious; rushing; impetuous; as, a fierce wind.
2. Savage; ravenous; easily enraged; as, a fierce lion.
3. Vehement in rage; eager of mischief; as, a fierce tyrant.
4. Very eager; ardent; as, fierce for the fight.
FIERCELY, adv. Violently; furiously; with rage.
FIERCENESS, n. Ferocity; savageness; keenness for blood; violence; fury; vehemence.
scriptures: Genesis 49:7
Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.
Deuteronomy 28:50
A nation of fierce countenance, which shall not regard the person of the old, nor shew favour to the young:
Isaiah 13:9
Behold, the day of the LORD cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate: and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it.
2 Timothy 3:3
Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good,
corruption_summary: Fierceness has been promoted into a virtue — fierce advocacy, fierce loyalty, fierce love — while Scripture lists it among the marks of the last days and curses it where it drives a man's anger.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage has turned fierce into praise. A man is commended for fierce conviction, a mother for fierce love, an advocate for fierce commitment to a cause. The Bible's vocabulary runs the other way. Jacob curses the fierceness of his sons' anger; Moses describes a nation of fierce countenance as a covenant curse, marked precisely by its refusal to spare the old and the young; and Paul lists fierce among the traits of perilous times, in company with trucebreaking and false accusation. Where zeal must be fierce to be felt, it has already left the gentleness the Apostle requires of the Lord's servant.

The corresponding error is to conclude that Christian love is therefore mild in the sense of weak, and that nothing is worth vehemence. Scripture does not teach it. There is a holy severity in the prophets, our Lord drove out the money-changers, and Isaiah 13:9 shows a divine anger against sin that is genuinely fierce. The distinction is the one Jacob drew: the object and the government of the passion, not its temperature. Anger at what God hates, ruled by His word and refusing cruelty to the weak, is righteous; a fierceness that regards neither the aged nor the young is under a curse, whatever cause it serves.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'az (strong, fierce) and charown (burning of anger) supply the Old Testament senses; Greek anemeros (not tame, savage) is the word in Paul's catalogue of the last days.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'az (H5794) — strong, mighty, fierce; used of a fierce anger and of strong nations.
Hebrew charown (H2740) — burning, heat of anger; the “fierce anger” of the day of the LORD in Isaiah 13:9.
Hebrew panim (H6440) — face, countenance; the fierce countenance of the judging nation in Deuteronomy 28:50.
Greek anemeros (G434) — not tame, savage, fierce; the last-days trait of 2 Timothy 3:3.
Greek chalepos (G5467) — hard, harsh, perilous; the adjective describing those same last times.
usage: “Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce” — the fierceness is condemned, not merely the anger.
“A nation of fierce countenance” — the mark is mercilessness toward the old and the young.
“Incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good” — fierceness belongs to the perilous times.

pos: adj. (causing terror; awful; dreadful; rendering Hebrew yare, 'ayom, Greek phoberos)
etymology: From Latin terribilis, from terreo, to frighten. In the Authorized Version the word means awe-inspiring rather than of poor quality, and it is applied to God as a title of honour, not of complaint.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version terrible means what inspires terror, and it is applied to God as praise. Moses sings it at the sea: “Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?” (Exodus 15:11), and the Psalms make the terror of His works the reason His enemies submit: “Say unto God, How terrible art thou in thy works! through the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies submit themselves unto thee” (Psalm 66:3). Nehemiah shows how naturally the word sits beside covenant faithfulness in prayer: “I beseech thee, O LORD God of heaven, the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy for them that love him and observe his commandments” (Nehemiah 1:5). The same God is terrible and keeps mercy, and the man praying sets the two side by side without apology. Joel fixes the word to the day of reckoning: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come” (Joel 2:31). Modern English has degraded the word to mean merely bad, which is why readers stumble here; the older sense is nearer to dreadful in its original force — full of dread, and rightly so.
webster_summary: Frightful; dreadful; adapted to excite terror; formidable; awful. In Scripture it is a title of honour for God, whose works and whose day are terrible, and never a term of mere disparagement.
webster_full: TERRIBLE, a. [L. terribilis, from terreo, to frighten.] Frightful; adapted to excite terror; dreadful; formidable.
2. Adapted to impress dread, awe or solemn reverence; as, the terrible majesty of God.
3. Severe; sharp; as, terrible discipline.
TERRIBLENESS, n. The quality or state of being terrible; dreadfulness; formidableness.
TERRIBLY, adv. In a manner to excite terror or fright; dreadfully; violently.
TERROR, n. Extreme fear; violent dread; fright; also, the cause of extreme fear.
scriptures: Exodus 15:11
Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?
Psalm 66:3
Say unto God, How terrible art thou in thy works! through the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies submit themselves unto thee.
Nehemiah 1:5
And said, I beseech thee, O LORD God of heaven, the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy for them that love him and observe his commandments:
Joel 2:31
The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come.
corruption_summary: The word has decayed in English until it means only bad, and with the word has gone the thing: a God whose works excite dread is thought incompatible with a God who keeps covenant and mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: Language shifts, and doctrine can drain out through the shift without anyone deciding anything. Terrible once meant awe-inspiring; it now means of poor quality, so that a modern ear hearing “the great and terrible God” registers something like an accusation. The loss is not merely lexical. When the vocabulary of dread disappears, the fear of the LORD — which Scripture calls the beginning of knowledge — has no words left to inhabit, and worship contracts to affection. Nehemiah felt no strain in addressing the terrible God who keeps covenant and mercy, and the strain a modern reader feels is a symptom worth naming.

The practical corruption follows: a religion in which God is admired but not feared, and in which Joel's great and terrible day is either allegorized away or quietly dropped from preaching. Scripture will not permit the edit. The same prophets who promise mercy announce the day; the same Moses who sang of steadfast love asked who is like the LORD, fearful in praises. Recover the older sense of the word and the older shape of worship returns with it — reverence and godly fear, in which mercy is precious exactly because the One showing it is terrible in His works.
roots_summary: Hebrew yare (to fear, to be awed) supplies the participle rendered terrible; 'ayom (dreadful, awesome) and Greek phoberos (fearful, terrible) complete the field.
roots_lines: Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear, revere, be awed; its participle is the “terrible” of Nehemiah 1:5 and Psalm 66:3.
Hebrew 'ayom (H366) — dreadful, terrible, awesome; used of an army terrible with banners.
Hebrew yir'ah (H3374) — fear, reverence; the disposition Scripture calls the beginning of wisdom.
Greek phoberos (G5398) — fearful, terrible; used of falling into the hands of the living God.
Greek epiphanes (G2016) — illustrious, notable, glorious; the Septuagint's word in Joel 2:31 for the terrible day.
usage: “How terrible art thou in thy works!” — the word is praise, not complaint.
“The great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy” — dread and covenant mercy sit together.
“The great and the terrible day of the LORD” — the reckoning is named before it comes.

pos: adj. (not high; humble in station; brought down; rendering Hebrew shaphal, Greek tapeinos)
etymology: From the Norse lagr, low. Scripture keeps the physical and the social senses joined to a moral one: the low place is where God characteristically works, and the high place is where He characteristically resists.
biblical_def: Low in Scripture is a station rather than a defect, and it is the station God prefers to work from. Mary's song states the principle as a settled divine habit: “He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree” (Luke 1:52). The two clauses are one action; the same providence that lowers the seated mighty raises the low. Job's friend, whatever else he got wrong, states the same rule rightly: God works “To set up on high those that be low; that those which mourn may be exalted to safety” (Job 5:11). The Psalmist writes it into Israel's history as a mercy remembered: “Who remembered us in our low estate: for his mercy endureth for ever” (Psalm 136:23). Low estate is not something the LORD overlooks but something He specifically remembers. James therefore turns the word into a command for rejoicing rather than a cause of shame: “Let the brother of low degree rejoice in that he is exalted” (James 1:9). The exaltation is present, not merely promised; a poor believer is already raised in Christ, and the Apostle instructs him to reckon it so while his circumstances still say otherwise.
webster_summary: Not high or elevated; depressed below the usual level; humble in rank or condition; dejected. Scripture treats low estate as the place God remembers, works from, and exalts, and warns against the high-mindedness that despises it.
webster_full: LOW, a. [Norm. lagr, low.] Not high or elevated; depressed below any given surface or place; as, low ground; a low situation.
2. Not rising to the usual height; as, a man of low stature.
3. Declining near the horizon; as, the sun is low.
4. Humble in rank or condition; in a state of subjection or inferiority; as, men of low degree.
5. Dejected; depressed in spirits; as, low spirits.
6. Moderate; not high in price; also, not loud; as, a low voice.
scriptures: Luke 1:52
He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.
Job 5:11
To set up on high those that be low; that those which mourn may be exalted to safety.
Psalm 136:23
Who remembered us in our low estate: for his mercy endureth for ever:
James 1:9
Let the brother of low degree rejoice in that he is exalted:
corruption_summary: Low estate is treated as a problem to be escaped rather than a place God remembers, and the church has largely adopted the world's scale of seats — platform, influence, and reach — which is exactly the scale the Magnificat says God inverts.
corruption_paragraphs: The Magnificat is sung in churches that are organized on the opposite principle. Mary announces a God who puts down the mighty from their seats and exalts them of low degree; the surrounding religious culture measures a ministry by the size of its seat — attendance, platform, reach, influence — and quietly assumes that God is doing His best work wherever the numbers are largest. The two scales cannot both be right. Scripture's consistent testimony is that God chooses the base things and the things that are despised, and that He resists the proud, which means the pursuit of a higher seat is a pursuit of the place where divine resistance is promised.

There is an answering error among the low themselves: to treat low estate as identity and grievance rather than as the place of a present exaltation. James forbids that reading. The brother of low degree is commanded to rejoice, and the ground of the rejoicing is stated in the perfect tense — he is exalted. His circumstances have not changed; his standing has. Recover both halves and the word does its proper work: no man need climb to be remembered, and no man may sulk in the place where God has promised to remember him.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaphal (to be low, to be brought low) supplies both the physical and the moral senses; Greek tapeinos (lowly, humble) is the New Testament word for low degree and for the humility God gives grace to.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaphal (H8213) — to be or become low, to be humbled; used of mountains made low and of the proud brought down.
Hebrew dal (H1800) — poor, weak, thin; the low man whom the law protects and the LORD defends.
Greek tapeinos (G5011) — lowly, of low degree, humble; the word of Luke 1:52 and James 1:9.
Greek tapeinoo (G5013) — to make low, to humble; the verb of humbling oneself under the mighty hand of God.
Greek hupsoo (G5312) — to lift up, to exalt; the counterpart action performed upon the low.
usage: “Exalted them of low degree” — the raising of the low and the putting down of the mighty are one act.
“Who remembered us in our low estate” — low estate is remembered, not overlooked.
“Let the brother of low degree rejoice in that he is exalted” — the exaltation is present, not merely future.

pos: adj. (little in size, number, or degree; rendering Hebrew qatan, daq, Greek mikros)
etymology: From Saxon smæl, slender or narrow. Scripture attaches enormous weight to small things — a still small voice, a day of small things, a very small helm — because God's method is regularly to work by what men would overlook.
biblical_def: Small in Scripture is rarely a dismissal. At Horeb the LORD passes by in wind, earthquake, and fire, and is in none of them; what remains is “a still small voice” (1 Kings 19:12), and that is where God is. The prophet had asked for vindication by spectacle and was answered by the opposite. Zechariah rebukes the contempt directly, and does so while a half-built temple stood as the evidence: “For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth” (Zechariah 4:10). The plummet in a builder's hand is a small sight, and the eyes of the LORD are upon it. Job's counsellor states the general rule of God's way with beginnings: “Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase” (Job 8:7). Small is also a diagnostic word, and one proverb turns it upon the man himself with disconcerting economy: “If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small” (Proverbs 24:10). Adversity does not create the smallness; it measures it.
webster_summary: Slender; thin; little in size, quantity, degree, or importance. Scripture invests small things with weight — the still small voice, the day of small things, the small beginning — and uses smallness of strength as a diagnosis revealed by adversity.
webster_full: SMALL, a. [Sax. smæl; G. schmal, narrow.] Slender; thin; fine; of little diameter; hence, in general, little in size or quantity.
2. Minute; slight; as, a small effort; a small matter.
3. Little in degree; as, small progress.
4. Being of little moment, weight or importance; as, it is a small matter.
5. Not loud; soft; gentle; as, a small voice.
6. Narrow; as, the small of the leg or back. SMALLNESS, n. Littleness of size, quantity, or importance.
scriptures: 1 Kings 19:12
And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
Zechariah 4:10

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
Job 8:7
Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase.
Proverbs 24:10
If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small.
corruption_summary: Scale has become the measure of divine approval, so that the day of small things is despised in practice by a church that reckons faithfulness by size and treats the still small voice as a stage in the story rather than the point of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Zechariah's question is not rhetorical decoration; it was addressed to men who had seen the first temple and wept at the second. The despising of small things is a permanent religious temptation, and it is now institutionalized. Ministries are assessed by attendance, reach, and growth curves, and a faithful congregation of eighty is quietly classed as a problem to be solved. Scripture's own accounting is different: the plummet in Zerubbabel's hand is watched by the eyes of the LORD which run to and fro through the whole earth. What is small is not therefore unobserved; it is observed by the only Eyes whose assessment is final.

The parallel error is to seek God in the spectacular and to miss Him in the ordinary means. Elijah at Horeb is the standing rebuke. Wind, earthquake, and fire pass, and the LORD is in none of them; the word comes in a still small voice. A religion of dramatic signs and continuing revelations repeats the prophet's mistake with none of his excuse, since the canon is closed and the ordinary means — the word preached, the ordinances, prayer — are precisely the small things God has appointed. Recover the pattern, and smallness stops being a discouragement and becomes a category of expectation.
roots_summary: Hebrew qatan (small, young, insignificant) and daq (thin, fine) supply the Old Testament senses; Greek mikros (small, little) and elachistos (least) carry them into the New.
roots_lines: Hebrew qatan (H6996) — small, little, young; the word of Zechariah's “day of small things”.
Hebrew daq (H1851) — thin, fine, small; used of the fine dust and of the still small voice at Horeb.
Hebrew demamah (H1827) — a whisper, a calm stillness; joined to daq in 1 Kings 19:12.
Greek mikros (G3398) — small, little; used of the mustard seed and of the little ones who believe.
Greek elachistos (G1646) — least, smallest; the measure of faithfulness in our Lord's parable of the talents.
usage: “A still small voice” — God was in what the spectacle had passed over.
“Who hath despised the day of small things?” — the question rebukes a permanent temptation.
“If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small” — trouble measures strength rather than creating weakness.

pos: adj. (of the colour of blood; rendering Hebrew 'adom, Greek purrhos)
etymology: From Saxon read, red. The colour is bound up with blood, with earth, and with the name Adam himself; Scripture uses it for guilt, for the sacrifice that cleanses guilt, and for the horse that takes peace from the earth.
biblical_def: Red is the colour of blood, and Scripture keeps it near both guilt and atonement. Isaiah sets it at the head of the gospel offer: “Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool” (Isaiah 1:18). The stain named is the deepest and most fixed dye known to the ancient world, and the promise is not that it will be lightened but that it will be made white. The ordinance of cleansing employs the same colour: “that they bring thee a red heifer without spot, wherein is no blemish, and upon which never came yoke” (Numbers 19:2), whose ashes made the water of purification for one defiled by death. Red also names an appetite that sold a birthright, and it gave a nation its name: “Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint: therefore was his name called Edom” (Genesis 25:30). Esau is remembered by the colour of a meal. In the Revelation the colour rides: “there went out another horse that was red: and power was given to him that sat thereon to take peace from the earth” (Revelation 6:4).
webster_summary: Of the colour of blood or of the ruby; one of the primary colours. Scripture makes it the colour of crimson guilt that God alone can whiten, of the red heifer whose ashes purified, of Esau's pottage, and of the horse that takes peace from the earth.
webster_full: RED, a. [Sax. read; D. rood; G. roth; L. rutilus.] Of a bright color, resembling blood; being one of the primary colors, of several shades or hues, as scarlet, crimson, vermilion.
2. Flushed with anger or shame; as, red with rage.
RED, n. A red color; the color resembling that of arterial blood.
REDDEN, v.t. To make red; v.i. to grow or become red; to blush.
REDDISH, a. Somewhat red; moderately red; tending to redness.
REDNESS, n. The quality of being red; red color.
scriptures: Isaiah 1:18
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
Numbers 19:2

This is the ordinance of the law which the LORD hath commanded, saying, Speak unto the children of Israel, that they bring thee a red heifer without spot, wherein is no blemish, and upon which never came yoke:
Genesis 25:30
And Esau said to Jacob, Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint: therefore was his name called Edom.
Revelation 6:4

And there went out another horse that was red: and power was given to him that sat thereon to take peace from the earth, and that they should kill one another: and there was given unto him a great sword.
corruption_summary: Isaiah's red-like-crimson has been softened into a promise of acceptance rather than of cleansing, so that the stain is declared unimportant instead of being made white.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 1:18 is quoted constantly and rarely finished. The verse is often used to say that God is reasonable and welcoming, which is true, and then the actual transaction is dropped. The prophet's claim is far stronger and far more offensive to modern sensibility: the sins are real, they are the colour of blood, they are fixed like the deepest dye, and God proposes to make them white as snow. A gospel that says the stain does not matter has not improved on that; it has removed the only sentence in which the stain is dealt with, and has left the guilty with reassurance instead of cleansing.

The red heifer supplies the answer to how such whitening is possible, and it is worth noticing how physical the provision is. A spotless animal, never yoked, is wholly consumed, and its ashes mixed with running water purify the man defiled by contact with death. Nothing about it is symbolic in the sense of unreal; it cost a life. Hebrews reasons from precisely this ordinance to the blood of Christ, arguing from the lesser cleansing to the greater. Recover the connection and the colour keeps its logic — red guilt is answered by red sacrifice, and only so does anyone come out white.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'adom (red) stands behind Edom, Adam, and adamah the ground; shani (scarlet) and towla (crimson) name the fixed dyes of Isaiah 1:18; Greek purrhos (fiery red) names the horse of Revelation 6:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'adom (H122) — red, ruddy; the root joining Edom, Adam, and adamah, the red ground.
Hebrew shani (H8144) — scarlet, crimson; one of the two fast dyes named in Isaiah 1:18.
Hebrew towla' (H8438) — worm, and the crimson dye made from it; the second dye of Isaiah 1:18.
Hebrew parah 'adummah — the red heifer of Numbers 19:2, whose ashes made the water of separation.
Greek purrhos (G4450) — fire-coloured, red; the colour of the second horse in Revelation 6:4.
usage: “Though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool” — the fastest dye is not lightened but made white.
“A red heifer without spot” — the cleansing from death's defilement cost a spotless life.
“Another horse that was red” — the colour of blood rides when peace is taken from the earth.

pos: adj. (having great sound; noisy; rendering Hebrew gadol, Greek megas)
etymology: From Saxon hlud, loud. Scripture never treats volume as a virtue in itself: the same adjective marks the praise of heaven, the cry of the dying Saviour, and the woman whose loudness is the mark of her folly.
biblical_def: Loud describes volume, and Scripture judges it entirely by what is being said. In worship it is commanded and commended: “the Levites… stood up to praise the LORD God of Israel with a loud voice on high” (2 Chronicles 20:19), and the song of heaven itself is loud — “Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing” (Revelation 5:12). Loudness there is proportion, not excess; the worth of the Lamb warrants the volume. The most solemn loud voice in Scripture is our Lord's at the moment of death: “And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost” (Luke 23:46). A crucified man ordinarily died in exhaustion; the loud cry testifies that He laid down His life rather than merely lost it. But volume can equally mark folly, and Proverbs uses the adjective as a character diagnosis of the strange woman: “She is loud and stubborn; her feet abide not in her house” (Proverbs 7:11). Loudness there is joined to stubbornness and restlessness as one disposition.
webster_summary: Having a great sound; noisy; striking the ear with force; clamorous. Scripture commends loud praise and records the loud cry of Christ at His death, while naming loudness joined to stubbornness as a mark of folly.
webster_full: LOUD, a. [Sax. hlud; G. laut.] Having a great sound; noisy; striking the ear with great force; as, a loud voice; a loud cry.
2. Clamorous; noisy; as, a loud man; loud complaints.
3. Emphatical; impressive; as, a loud call for repentance.
LOUDLY, adv. With great sound or noise; noisily; also, clamorously; importunately.
LOUDNESS, n. Great sound or noise; as the loudness of a voice or of thunder.
2. Clamor; turbulence; uproar.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 20:19
And the Levites, of the children of the Kohathites, and of the children of the Korhites, stood up to praise the LORD God of Israel with a loud voice on high.
Revelation 5:12
Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing.
Luke 23:46
And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost.
Proverbs 7:11
(She is loud and stubborn; her feet abide not in her house:
corruption_summary: Volume has been mistaken for fervour, so that intensity of sound is read as intensity of devotion in worship and as strength of conviction in argument — neither of which Scripture grants.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture commends loud praise and never equates loudness with sincerity. The Levites lifted their voices because of what they were saying, and the heavenly song is loud because the Lamb is worthy; in both cases the volume is answerable to the object. Where loudness becomes the instrument for producing feeling rather than the overflow of conviction about a Person, the order is inverted and worship begins to depend on the sound rather than on the truth. The test is simple enough to apply: remove the volume, and see whether anything is left that a congregation would still call worship.

The same confusion has moved into speech about doctrine, where volume and vehemence substitute for argument. Proverbs 7:11 is worth weighing here, since the loudness of the strange woman is listed as one symptom among a cluster — loud, stubborn, and never at home — which together sketch a character rather than a decibel level. Scripture's own model runs the other way: the still small voice at Horeb, a Servant who does not cry nor lift up his voice in the street, and a Saviour whose one recorded loud cry from the cross was a committal of His spirit into His Father's hands.
roots_summary: Hebrew idiom has no separate adjective for loud; it says qowl gadol, a great voice, and Greek follows with phone megale — the same construction rendered “loud voice” throughout the Authorized Version.
roots_lines: Hebrew qowl (H6963) — voice, sound, noise; the word joined to gadol to make a loud voice.
Hebrew gadol (H1419) — great, large; supplying the “loud” of a great voice in Hebrew idiom.
Hebrew hamah (H1993) — to murmur, roar, be clamorous; the verb behind the loud and stubborn woman of Proverbs 7:11.
Greek phone (G5456) — a voice, a sound; the noun in every “loud voice” of the New Testament.
Greek megas (G3173) — great; joined to phone for the loud cry of Luke 23:46 and Revelation 5:12.
usage: “Praise the LORD God of Israel with a loud voice on high” — volume answerable to its object is commended.
“When Jesus had cried with a loud voice” — the strength of the cry testifies that He laid down His life.
“She is loud and stubborn” — loudness joined to stubbornness sketches a character, not a volume.

pos: adj. (destitute of moisture; arid; rendering Hebrew yabesh, tsiyah, Greek xeros)
etymology: From Saxon drige, dry. Dryness in Scripture is the condition God delights to reverse: dry ground becomes a highway, dry bones become an army, and a root out of dry ground becomes the Saviour of the world.
biblical_def: Dry names the absence of water, and Scripture uses it as the standing picture of death, barrenness, and need — always as the setting for a divine reversal. At Jordan the dryness is deliverance: “the priests that bare the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firm on dry ground in the midst of Jordan, and all the Israelites passed over on dry ground” (Joshua 3:17). What ought to have been a riverbed became a road. In Ezekiel dryness is the condition of the dead, and the prophet is told to preach to it: “Prophesy upon these bones, and say unto them, O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD” (Ezekiel 37:4). Preaching to what cannot hear is exactly the commission, because the word does the raising. The promise turns the imagery to the Spirit: “For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring” (Isaiah 44:3). Most striking of all, the Messiah Himself grows in such soil: “he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him” (Isaiah 53:2).
webster_summary: Destitute of moisture; free from water or wetness; arid; barren. Scripture makes dryness the setting of God's reversals — dry ground for a highway, dry bones for an army, dry ground for the Root of Jesse, and floods promised upon the dry.
webster_full: DRY, a. [Sax. drige.] Destitute of moisture; free from water or wetness; arid; not moist; as, dry land; dry clothes.
2. Not rainy; as, dry weather; a dry season.
3. Barren; jejune; plain; unembellished; as, a dry style; a dry discourse.
4. Thirsty; craving drink.
5. Severe; sarcastic; wiping one; as, a dry rebuke.
DRY, v.t. To free from water or moisture; to exsiccate; v.i. to grow dry; to lose moisture; to evaporate wholly.
scriptures: Joshua 3:17

And the priests that bare the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firm on dry ground in the midst of Jordan, and all the Israelites passed over on dry ground, until all the people were passed clean over Jordan.
Ezekiel 37:4
Again he said unto me, Prophesy upon these bones, and say unto them, O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD.
Isaiah 44:3
For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring:
Isaiah 53:2
For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
corruption_summary: Spiritual dryness is now treated as a condition to be managed by technique or diagnosed as a defect of temperament, rather than as the very ground on which Scripture promises God pours water and raises the dead.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 37 addresses a valley of bones that are not merely dead but dry — long dead, past any hope of natural recovery — and the remedy is not a method but a word preached to them. Much modern counsel about spiritual dryness runs the other way, prescribing adjustments of routine, atmosphere, or personality, as though the condition were a mood to be corrected by better inputs. Where the diagnosis is wrong the remedy will be trivial. Scripture's answer to dryness is the word of the LORD and the outpoured Spirit, and its promise is aimed precisely at the dry ground rather than at the ground that is doing tolerably well.

Isaiah 53:2 forbids the further error of despising dry soil. The Messiah grew up as a root out of a dry ground, without form or comeliness, and men did not desire Him for it. A church that judges by comeliness will always misjudge such beginnings and will look for God's work in fertile-looking places. Recover the pattern that runs from Jordan to the valley of bones to the Root of Jesse: dryness is not the absence of God's working but the customary setting of it, and the floods are promised to the thirsty rather than to the watered.
roots_summary: Hebrew yabesh (to be dry, withered) describes the bones and the dried-up sea; tsiyah (drought, dry land) names the parched place; Greek xeros (dry, withered) carries the sense into the New Testament.
roots_lines: Hebrew yabesh (H3001) — to be dry, to wither; the adjective describing the bones in Ezekiel 37:4.
Hebrew charabah (H2724) — dry ground, dry land; the ground on which Israel crossed Jordan in Joshua 3:17.
Hebrew tsiyah (H6723) — dryness, drought, a parched land; the setting of the soul's thirst in the Psalms.
Hebrew tsiyyah — the dry ground out of which the Servant grows in Isaiah 53:2.
Greek xeros (G3584) — dry, withered; used of the withered hand and of the dry tree in our Lord's warning.
usage: “All the Israelites passed over on dry ground” — the riverbed became the road.
“O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD” — preaching to what cannot hear is the commission.
“As a root out of a dry ground” — the Messiah grew where nothing was expected to grow.

pos: v. & n. (to squander or lay desolate; a desolation; rendering Hebrew chorbah, shamem, Greek diaskorpizo, apoleia)
etymology: From Latin vastus, empty or desolate. Scripture uses the word for a city in ruins and for a fortune squandered, and answers both with the same promise of rebuilding.
biblical_def: Waste is both a state and an act: a place laid desolate, and a substance squandered. Nehemiah names the first when he moves men to build: “Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Nehemiah 2:17). The waste is not accepted as permanent; it is stated plainly and then answered with labour. Isaiah turns the same noun into a promise of restoration on a generational scale: “And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations” (Isaiah 61:4). What was ruined for generations is not beyond rebuilding. The active sense appears in the prodigal, and the verb carries the whole moral weight of the parable's first movement: “the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living” (Luke 15:13). Our Lord also records the word being used wrongly, by men who called an act of costly devotion a waste: “Why was this waste of the ointment made?” (Mark 14:4). What indignant men called waste, He called a good work.
webster_summary: To diminish by gradual dissipation; to squander; to desolate or lay in ruins; also, a desert or ruined place. Scripture pairs the ruin with the promise of rebuilding, names the prodigal's squandering, and corrects those who called costly devotion a waste.
webster_full: WASTE, v.t. [L. vastus, empty, desolate.] To diminish by gradual dissipation or loss; to squander; to expend without necessity or use; as, to waste an estate.
2. To destroy in enmity; to desolate; to lay waste; as, to waste a country by fire and sword.
3. To wear out; to consume; as, disease wastes the body.
WASTE, v.i. To dwindle; to be diminished; to be consumed by degrees.
WASTE, a. Desolate; uncultivated; destroyed; ruined; as, waste places.
WASTE, n. The act of squandering; loss; destruction; also, a desert; a region ruined and uninhabited.
scriptures: Nehemiah 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
Isaiah 61:4
And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations.
Luke 15:13
And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.
Mark 14:4
And there were some that had indignation within themselves, and said, Why was this waste of the ointment made?
corruption_summary: The word is now applied chiefly to inefficiency, so that costly worship is judged wasteful by the same reasoning the disciples used at Bethany, while genuine squandering of a life is called self-discovery.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 14:4 records the only people in the Gospels who used the word waste about an act of worship, and our Lord contradicted them flatly. The reasoning behind their indignation was impeccable by ordinary standards — the ointment could have been sold and the money given to the poor — and it is precisely the reasoning a church adopts whenever beauty, reverence, and costliness in worship are assessed purely by utility. Scripture does not despise the poor; it commands care for them constantly. What it refuses is the calculation that treats devotion to Christ as an inefficiency to be trimmed.

The opposite corruption renames real waste. The prodigal wasted his substance with riotous living, and a far country full of such young men would today describe the same years as finding themselves. The parable is not sentimental about it: the substance was genuinely gone, the famine was real, and the son came to himself only when he was in want. Yet the same chapter and Isaiah 61:4 together are the answer to despair over it. What has been laid waste for generations may be rebuilt, and the father runs while the son is yet a great way off.
roots_summary: Hebrew chorbah (a desolation, waste place) and shamem (to be desolate) supply the ruin; Greek diaskorpizo (to scatter, squander) gives the prodigal's act and apoleia (loss, destruction) the disciples' complaint.
roots_lines: Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a waste, desolation, ruin; the “old wastes” to be rebuilt in Isaiah 61:4.
Hebrew shamem (H8074) — to be desolate, appalled; the verb behind the desolations of many generations.
Hebrew charab (H2717) — to be dry, to lie waste; the state of Jerusalem in Nehemiah 2:17.
Greek diaskorpizo (G1287) — to scatter abroad, to squander; the prodigal's wasting in Luke 15:13.
Greek apoleia (G684) — loss, waste, destruction; the word the indignant used of the ointment in Mark 14:4.
usage: “Jerusalem lieth waste” — the ruin is named plainly and then answered with building.
“They shall build the old wastes” — desolations of many generations are not beyond repair.
“Why was this waste of the ointment made?” — costly devotion looked like waste to reasonable men.
